stances.claim: The pivotal issue in Duterte's ICC case is whether the two-year prescriptive period runs from Bensouda's unilateral preliminary examination start or only from her formal application or the Pre-Trial Chamber's grant of authority.
stances.rhetorical_move: issue framing restated for the reading public

stances.claim: Under the 2023 PH doctrine in Republic v. Desierto and Corpuz Jr. v. People, prescription is tolled only when the information is filed in court -- not when the complaint is filed at the prosecutor's office.
stances.rhetorical_move: summary of the now-superseded PH rule

stances.claim: The argument that prescription should run from Bensouda's February 8, 2018 preliminary examination relies on the OP being an integral organ of the ICC itself -- unlike the PH DOJ, which is in the executive branch.
People v. Consebido (April 2, 2025, per J. Inting, en banc) abandoned the old doctrine and now treats the filing of the complaint with PH prosecutors as the tolling event.

Applying Consebido analogously to the ICC scenario means the two-year window had not even begun running because Bensouda started her examination while the PH was still an ICC member -- so prescription does not apply and Duterte's case should not be dismissed.
The recent doctrinal 'somersault' is a double-edged sword: it could keep Duterte detained in The Hague while it prolongs cases in the Philippines.

one_paragraph_summary: Returning to a topic he addressed on March 24, Panganiban explains how the question of prescription operates in the case of former president Rodrigo R. Duterte at the International Criminal Court and how recent Philippine jurisprudence affects it. He restates the pivotal issue: the ICC Statute gives the Office of the Prosecutor two years from the Philippines' withdrawal (effective March 17, 2019) to conduct its preliminary examination and seek Pre-Trial Chamber authority to investigate; former ICC Chief Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda started her preliminary examination on February 8, 2018 (when the PH was still a member), applied for formal investigation only on May 24, 2021, and received Pre-Trial Chamber authority on September 15, 2021 -- both well past the two-year limit. Under the now-superseded PH rule in Republic v. Desierto (January 16, 2023) and Corpuz Jr. v. People (August 16, 2023), prescription was tolled only when the information was filed in court, not when the complaint was filed at the prosecutor's office; the ICC counterargument was that the OP is an integral organ of the ICC itself (alongside the Presidency, Judicial Divisions, and Registry), unlike the PH DOJ, which sits in the executive branch. But in People v. Consebido (April 2, 2025, per J. Henri Jean Paul B. Inting, en banc), the Supreme Court abandoned the old doctrine and now treats the filing of the complaint at the DOJ or city/provincial prosecutor's office as the tolling event, reasoning that 'it is unjust to deprive the injured party of the right to obtain vindication on account of delays that are not under [their] control.' Applying that analogously, Duterte's ICC case should not be dismissed because the two-year window had not even begun running when Bensouda started her examination while the PH was still a member. He closes by noting the doctrinal 'somersault' is double-edged: it explains how prescription could end Duterte's detention in The Hague while it could also prolong his case in Philippine courts.
